## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The authors set out to estimate the causal effect of adopting Cursor, which they call "a widely popular LLM agent assistant" [V], on development velocity and software quality, because practitioners report multifold productivity gains while "empirical evidence is lacking around these claims" [V] (Abstract, p. 1) [AR]. They argue that earlier findings on code completion and chat-based tools cannot simply carry over to agentic assistants that edit many files autonomously: the architectural difference has implications "that cannot be extrapolated from prior studies" [V] (§1, p. 1) [AR]. Their research question asks how adopting LLM agent assistants affects project-level development velocity and code quality (§1, p. 2) [AP].

Using a staggered difference-in-differences design that compares Cursor-adopting GitHub projects with a propensity-matched control group, they find that adopting Cursor brings "a statistically significant, large, but transient increase in project-level development velocity" [V], together with "a substantial and persistent increase in static analysis warnings and code complexity" [V] (Abstract, p. 1) [AE]. Panel generalized-method-of-moments (GMM) models indicate that rises in warnings and complexity are major factors driving later velocity slowdown, so that accumulated technical debt "subsequently reduces future velocity, creating a self-reinforcing cycle" [V] (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2) [AE]. Cursor adoption still raises code complexity when the models control for velocity dynamics (§1, p. 2) [AE].

From this they conclude that quality assurance is a major bottleneck for early Cursor adopters, and call for it to be a first-class citizen in the design of agentic AI coding tools and AI-driven workflows (Abstract, p. 1) [AR]. For practitioners, they write, "deliberate process adaptations—those that scale quality assurance with AI-era velocity—are necessary to realize sustained benefits from the use of LLM agent assistants" [V] (§1, p. 2) [AR]. They state that their evidence "challenges both unbridled optimism and categorical pessimism" [V] about AI-assisted coding, and they list reasons the picture may be less bleak than it first appears (§6, p. 11) [AR].

The authors tie their estimates to their setting. The sample is open-source GitHub repositories with at least 10 stars that committed Cursor configuration files, adopting mostly between August 2024 and March 2025 and observed from January 2024 to August 2025 (§1, p. 2; §3.1.2, p. 4; §3.2, p. 5) [AE]. The authors read their estimates as intent-to-treat effects of visible adoption, measured against a state of practice in which other AI tools may already be in use, not against no AI use (§3.5.1, p. 7) [AR].

## Part I: The question and the prior evidence

### Why agentic assistants need their own study (§1, pp. 1–2)

LLM agent assistants combine LLMs with autonomous capabilities to inspect project files, execute commands and iteratively develop code (§1, p. 1) [AP]. Cursor has drawn enthusiasm, with developers self-reporting multifold productivity increases (as large as 10x) [BT] (§1, p. 1). Studies have documented that AI coding assistants can produce code with security vulnerabilities, performance issues, code smells and increased complexity, but those findings came from early Codex models in controlled experiments, completion-based tools like early GitHub Copilot, or chat interfaces like ChatGPT [BT] (§1, p. 1). The authors argue such findings may not generalize to modern agent assistants, which they describe as a qualitative shift in architecture and integration, not an incremental improvement (§1, p. 1) [AR].

Completion tools suggest individual lines from immediate context, and chat assistants require context-switching; both sit at the periphery of the workflow, with developers remaining the primary agents and overseeing AI-generated code at a granular level (§1, p. 1) [AR]. Cursor, by contrast, is integrated into the IDE with persistent codebase awareness, navigating files, proposing multi-file refactorings and implementing features spanning dozens of files (§1, p. 1) [AR]. The authors list what follows: automation scope shifts from accelerating typing to automating entire workflows; seamless integration may bring both productivity gains and over-reliance or reduced code review rigor; reviewing large AI-generated multi-file changes differs from reviewing line-by-line completions; and longer-term effects such as technical debt accumulation may appear (§1, pp. 1–2) [AR].

They point to a gap between tool generations in recent research. Becker et al. found in controlled experiments that early-2025 AI tools, Cursor among them, did not help experienced open-source developers solve real day-to-day tasks faster, pointing to potential slowdown mechanisms such as developer over-optimism, low AI reliability and high task complexity, which contradicts the prior literature's generally modest velocity improvements from completion tools [BT] (§1, p. 2). Watanabe et al. examined 567 pull requests generated by Claude Code and found 83.8% accepted and merged, but analysed acceptance rates and task types, not longitudinal project-level effects [BT] (§1, p. 2). Whether high acceptance of individual agent-generated PRs translates into sustained productivity and maintained quality at project level, or whether quality degradation accumulates over months, is in the authors' framing an open empirical question (§1, p. 2) [AR].

### Prior productivity and quality evidence (§2, pp. 2–3)

The 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey reports that 76% of respondents use or plan to use LLM tools in development [BT] (§2, p. 2). Most prior productivity research studies pre-agentic GitHub Copilot [BT] (§2, pp. 2–3). Small, constrained randomized experiments report productivity increases from 21% to 56% in task completion time; field experiments at Microsoft, Accenture and Cisco report 22% to 36% [BT] (§2, p. 3). Observational estimates from open source are similar or lower: a DiD comparison of Python and R packages estimates a 17.82% increase in new Python package releases after Copilot became available, without knowing which packages used it; a study of proprietary Copilot backend data estimates a 6.5% rise in project-level productivity measured by accepted pull requests; and a neural-classifier study finds that moving to 30% AI use raises quarterly commits by 2.4% [BT] (§2, p. 3).

On quality, LLMs may generate code with security vulnerabilities, performance regressions, code smells and outdated APIs, while evidence on the complexity of LLM-generated code compared with human code is inconclusive [BT] (§2, p. 3). Controlled experiments give mixed results on whether developers write more or less secure code with LLM help, and studies often suggest effects differ by developer skill [BT] (§2, p. 3). The authors write, "We are unaware of any prior studies that systematically investigated project-level quality outcomes in the wild after LLM adoption" [V], the closest being Yeverechyahu et al. (§2, p. 3) [AR].

Gray literature carries optimistic estimates, such as multifold self-reported productivity boosts in a Reddit post, which the authors describe as orders of magnitude larger than any empirical estimate for prior LLM tools; a controlled study suggests developers may be over-optimistic and that agent assistants do not make them faster on real open-source tasks [BT] (§2, p. 3). The authors state a two-fold contribution: a DiD estimate of the additional project-level productivity gain, if any, from a modern agentic assistant relative to the state of practice (likely a mixture of human-written code and code from earlier AI tools); and, to their knowledge, the first comprehensive analysis of Cursor adoption's effect on code quality, highlighting potential velocity-quality trade-offs (§2, p. 3) [AR].

## Part II: Research design

### The Cursor IDE and why it was chosen (§3.1.1, p. 3)

Cursor is an AI-powered IDE built as a VS Code fork; its agentic mode can navigate codebases, infer architecture across files, make multi-file edits, run terminal commands, execute tests and iteratively debug, "with humans mainly serving as supervisors rather than traditional coders" [V] (§3.1.1, p. 3) [AP]. Developers can choose frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google (§3.1.1, p. 3) [AP]. The authors chose Cursor because their preliminary exploration found widespread and growing adoption, giving statistical power, and because Cursor was among the earliest tools to allow optional configuration files (e.g. `.cursorrules`) in the git repository, which leave an adoption timestamp in version control (§3.1.1, pp. 3–4) [AR].

### Identifying adopters (§3.1.2, p. 4; §1, p. 2)

The first commit touching Cursor configuration files serves as a proxy for the adoption date of the modern Cursor client with agentic features (§1, p. 2) [AR]. Footnote 1 explains that Cursor rule files appeared in mid-2024, about when the Composer feature (a conversational interface for multi-file generation) did, and that Composer's agentic features were released in November 2024 and made default in February 2025 [BT] (§1, fn. 1, p. 2). So the identification captures a mix of Composer's multi-file editing and the later default agent mode, which the paper calls simply "Cursor" for brevity (§1, fn. 1, p. 2) [AR].

Querying the GitHub code search API for `.cursorrules` files or `.cursor` folders, with an adaptive file-size partitioning algorithm to get past the 1,000-result limit, found 23,308 Cursor files across 3,306 non-fork repositories as of March 2025 (§3.1.2, p. 4) [AE]. To filter non-software, educational, toy and spam repositories, the authors required at least 10 stars, a threshold reported to achieve 97% precision in identifying engineered projects [BT]; this left 806 repositories with adoption dates between January 2024 and March 2025, still available in August 2025 (§3.1.2, p. 4) [AE]. Most adoptions fall between August 2024 and March 2025 (§1, p. 2) [AE]. The dataset is highly skewed (Table 1) and adoption is staggered and growing over time (Figure 2) (§3.1.2, p. 4) [AE]. The top primary languages are TypeScript (366), Python (118), JavaScript (60), Go (36) and Rust (24) (§3.1.2, p. 4) [AE].

### Building the control group (§3.1.3, pp. 4–5; Appendix A, p. 14)

Because adopters may be more active, more rapidly growing and have larger communities than random never-adopters, the authors use propensity score matching against a population of all GitHub repositories with at least 10 stars, using monthly GHArchive time series (age, active users, stars, forks, releases, pull requests, issues, comments, total events) for each month with major adoptions, August 2024 to March 2025 (§3.1.3, p. 4) [AE]. The logistic propensity model includes repository age, six months of month-by-month lags and cumulative earlier history, so that scores reflect both activity level and trajectory (§3.1.3, p. 4) [AE]. Sampling at most 10,000 candidates per adoption month, the models reach AUC values from 0.83 to 0.91 (§3.1.3, pp. 4–5) [AE]. Each adopter gets three nearest-neighbour controls with the same primary language, chosen over 1:1 because many adopters matched the same control (§3.1.3, p. 5) [AE]. The intro reports 1,380 matched never-adopter repositories (§1, p. 2) [AE].

Appendix A gives the per-cohort figures: 762,968 to 818,160 candidate repositories; AUC 0.8281 to 0.9144; McFadden's pseudo R² 0.1412 to 0.2722, which the authors read as the covariates explaining only 14.12% to 27.22% of the variance, an expected result since adoption decisions are "probably not driven by any observable information in GitHub" [V] (Appendix A, Table 4, p. 14) [AE]. The matched controls are slightly skewed toward lower propensity scores (Figure 5), and all covariates show acceptable balance (|Norm. Diff| < 0.25), yet observable mean differences remain; the authors say this "indicates that our matching is imperfect" [V], which motivates the DiD design over a direct comparison of outcomes (Appendix A, p. 14) [AR]. In Table 5, the largest normalized difference is repository age (−0.207; treatment mean 496.07 days, control 681.38) (Table 5, p. 14) [AE].

### Outcomes and covariates (§3.2, p. 5)

Monthly metrics run from January 2024 to August 2025, giving at least six months before and after adoption for the treatment group; the panel is unbalanced (§3.2, p. 5) [AE]. Velocity outcomes are commits and lines added per repository-month, both used as productivity proxies with moderate-to-strong correlation with perceived productivity [BT] (§3.2.1, p. 5). Taking a technical-debt perspective, the authors measure three maintainability metrics with a local SonarQube Community server: static analysis warnings (reliability, maintainability and security issues, called warnings because static analysis can produce false positives, and to be read "as an estimate of the effort required to review potential issues in a project" [V]); duplicate line density; and code complexity, measured as SonarQube's cognitive complexity of the codebase (§3.2.1, p. 5) [AE]. All three are, they argue, positively correlated with technical debt and negatively with perceived quality (§3.2.1, p. 5) [AR]. Time-varying covariates are lines of code, age, contributors, stars and issues opened; issue comments were dropped for collinearity with issues (Pearson's ρ > 0.7) (§3.2.2, p. 5) [AE].

### Difference-in-differences and the Borusyak estimator (§3.3, pp. 5–7)

DiD compares outcome changes in the treatment group with those in a control group over the same periods, isolating the intervention's effect from other factors that affect all repositories similarly, such as macro trends like open-source repositories overall getting more or less active (§3, p. 3; §3.3.1, p. 5) [AR]. A causal reading rests on the parallel trends assumption, which is not directly testable but is checked with pre-trend tests and made more plausible by matching (§3.3.1, p. 5) [AR]. Staggered adoption lets later adopters serve as controls for earlier ones but complicates unbiased estimation (§3.3.1, p. 5) [BT]. The targets are ATT, the average effect on treated observations, and ATT_h, the "horizon-average" effect h months after adoption (§3.3.2, pp. 5–6) [AE].

Because two-way fixed effects (TWFE) may give biased estimates under staggered adoption when effects vary over time, the authors use the Borusyak et al. imputation estimator: fit a counterfactual outcome model with per-repository and per-month fixed effects and time-varying covariates on untreated observations only, then compare actual with imputed outcomes after adoption [BT] (§3.3.3, p. 6). Pre-trends are tested with heteroscedasticity- and cluster-robust Wald tests on placebo estimates for h = −k to −2; h = −1 is dropped for possible anticipation, since a developer may try Cursor before adding rule files (§3.3.3, p. 6) [AE]. Results from TWFE and Callaway and Sant'Anna estimators appear in Appendix B (§3.3.3, p. 6) [AE]. All outcomes are log-transformed, so an ATT reads as a percentage change of 100(e^ATT − 1)% (Table 2, p. 7) [AE].

### Velocity-quality interaction models (§3.4, pp. 6–7)

DiD does not capture dynamics between outcomes, and the DiD results themselves suggest that velocity increases may cause rapid technical debt accumulation, which may later decrease velocity (§3.4, p. 6) [AR]. To test this the authors fit Arellano-Bond dynamic panel GMM models, which use lagged values as instruments for potentially endogenous regressors, with a Cursor-adoption dummy and the covariates [BT] (§3.4, p. 6). They test four paths: lines added → warnings; lines added → complexity; warnings → next month's lines added; complexity → next month's lines added (§3.4, p. 6, Eq. 7) [AE].

## Part III: Threats to validity the authors state

### Internal validity (§3.5.1, p. 7)

The authors "advise readers to interpret our results in the context of this experimental setup and its limitations" [V] (§3.5.1, p. 7) [AR]. They name five limitations (§3.5.1, p. 7) [AR]:

- *Observable adoption through committed configuration files.* Developers can use Cursor without committing such files, so the sample is repositories with observable adoption, a potential selection bias. If committed adopters use Cursor more systematically, estimates may be an upper bound; if they are more quality-conscious, estimates could be conservative. The authors view the sample as repositories where adoption represents deliberate, visible practice change, "precisely the population where long-term effects are most relevant" [V].
- *Uncertainty about usage intensity and persistence.* A `.cursorrules` file "only indicates someone experimented, not that all contributors used it continuously" [V]; contributors may use Cursor for one feature and revert without trace. Usage is assumed to continue unless removal is observed, so "our main estimates represent intent-to-treat (ITT) effects" [V].
- *Model and version heterogeneity.* The data lack which Cursor version or LLM backend each repository used; the authors argue this does not compromise validity, because the question is the system-level effect of adopting an agentic assistant as practised, and the mix increases external validity.
- *Imperfect matching.* Even at AUC 0.83–0.91, unobserved confounders such as developer expertise, team practices, project complexity or organizational culture may affect both adoption and outcomes; matching is meant to strengthen the parallel trends assumption, not to create two directly comparable groups, and fixed effects and covariates address the remainder (§3.5.1, p. 7).
- *Contamination from alternative AI coding tools.* Treatment and control repositories may use Copilot or chat interfaces without trace, so the estimates are of systematic Cursor adoption compared with the current state of practice, "not the impact of using Cursor with respect to no AI usage at all" [V].

### External validity (§3.5.2, p. 7)

Results may not generalize to other LLM agent assistants, to proprietary software, or to languages beyond the three dominant ones in the dataset (JavaScript, TypeScript, Python) (§3.5.2, p. 7) [AR]. The study period coincides with rapid change in LLM capabilities, agent tooling and adoption patterns, and "Results observed may not persist as LLM agent assistants mature and developer workflows adapt" [V] (§3.5.2, p. 7) [AR].

### Further limits stated elsewhere in the paper

- The quality findings depend on the estimator; given small cohorts and no clear guidance on time-varying covariates, "the findings around code quality outcomes should be interpreted with appropriate caution" [V] (Appendix B.3, p. 16) [AR].
- The identification cannot clearly separate developers using the older Composer feature from those using the later agentic features; most repositories probably mix autonomy levels (Appendix C, p. 17) [AR].
- The dataset does not sufficiently cover Java, C/C++ and Rust, where outcomes might differ (Appendix C, p. 16) [AR].
- The SonarQube warning sample in Appendix D "is merely a convenience sample" [V], used only descriptively (Appendix D, p. 18) [AR].
- Complexity metrics were designed for human-written code, and whether they appropriately penalize AI-generated patterns that are mechanically verifiable yet syntactically complex remains open (§6, p. 11) [AR].

## Part IV: Results

### Development velocity (§4.1.1, p. 8; Table 2, p. 7; §1, p. 2)

All outcomes pass the pre-trend Wald tests at the 0.05 level (§4.1, pp. 7–8) [AE]. On average, adoption has what the authors call a "modestly significant positive impact on development velocity" [V], concentrated in code volume: lines added rise by about 28.6% (Table 2: +28.58% ±13.7%, p < 0.05) (§4.1.1, p. 8) [AE]. "There is no statistically significant effect for the volume of commits." [V] (§4.1.1, p. 8) [AE].

The horizon estimates show the timing: "The only significant development velocity gain is in the first two months post Cursor adoption." [V] (§4.1.1, p. 8). The models estimate a 55.4% rise in commits in the first month and 14.5% in the second, and a 281.3% rise in lines added in the first month and 48.4% in the second (§4.1.1, p. 8) [AE]. The introduction summarises this as "3-5x increases in lines added in the first adoption month" [V], with gains dissipating after two months (§1, p. 2) [AE].

### Software quality (§4.1.2, p. 8; Table 2, p. 7)

Static analysis warnings rise significantly by 30.3% and code complexity by 41.6% on average; the effect on duplicate line density is not significant (§4.1.2, p. 8) [AE]. The horizon estimates show the rise in warnings and complexity persisting beyond the initial adoption period, in contrast to the transient velocity gains (§4.1.2, p. 8) [AE].

### Velocity-quality interactions (§4.2, p. 8; Table 3, p. 8)

All four GMM models pass the Sargan and AR(2) tests (§4.2 and Table 3, p. 8) [AE]. Following Arellano and Bond [22], the authors interpret these tests as validating the moment conditions required for causal interpretation (§4.2, p. 8) [BT]. On average across adopters and non-adopters, holding other dynamics constant: a rise in velocity has no significant effect on warnings or complexity; Cursor adoption has no significant effect on warnings; and growth in codebase size is a major determinant of both, absorbing most of their variance (§4.2, p. 8) [AE]. Even with those controls, adoption has a significant effect on complexity, "a 9% baseline increase on average compared to projects in similar dynamics but not using Cursor" [V] (§4.2, p. 8) [AE].

In the other direction, a 100% increase in code complexity and in static analysis warnings causes, in the authors' words, a 64.5% and a 50.3% decrease in lines added respectively, while adoption brings "a 1.84x baseline increase in lines added post adoption" [V] (§4.2, p. 8) [AE]. By these estimates the velocity gain would be fully cancelled by a ∼5x rise in warnings or a ∼3x rise in complexity (§4.2, p. 8) [AE]. Their summary: Cursor adoption "leads to an inherently more complex codebase" [V], and accumulated warnings and complexity decrease future velocity (§4.2, p. 8) [AR].

### Robustness checks (§4.3, pp. 9–10; Appendix C, pp. 16–17)

*Usage intensity.* Two subsets test whether the findings come from genuine sustained use: High Contributor Adoption (repositories where contributors who modified Cursor files made ≥80% of commits) and Cursor Configuration Changes (post-adoption months with at least one commit modifying Cursor files) (§4.3, p. 9) [AE]. The quality findings are robust and amplified in these subsets; the warning and complexity build-up is "stronger—not weaker" [V] where configuration was refined and Cursor users dominated activity, which the authors say strengthens the causal reading and suggests the ITT estimates understate effects under intensive use (§4.3, p. 9) [AR]. The velocity gain stays transient on average in high-adoption repositories, but a velocity increase still appears in months when developers are modifying Cursor files, which "indicates that abandonments of Cursor post-adoption likely nullify at least part of the velocity gains" [V] (§4.3, p. 9) [AR].

*Activity level.* To test whether the transient gain only reflects repositories going inactive fast, subsets keep repository-months with at least one commit and with at least 10 commits; the main findings persist in very active repositories, weaker than the main estimates, which the authors expect given larger baselines (§4.3, p. 9) [AE].

*Other AI tools.* Taking what they call "an overly conservative approach" [V], the authors flag 382 treatment repositories that may use other AI tools based on repository files: 345 GitHub Copilot, 63 Claude Code, 37 Windsurf, 13 Cline and 2 OpenHands, overlapping heavily (§4.3, pp. 9–10) [AE]. Contamination weakens the estimates, but the main findings persist in all three settings and are amplified where prior AI tool use is less likely (§4.3, p. 10) [AE]. The authors conclude the checks reassure the main findings against non-compliance, selection bias from repositories going inactive, and confounding from other tools (§4.3, p. 10) [AR].

*Language and cohort (Appendix C).* Findings are qualitatively consistent across JavaScript/TypeScript, Python and Go; the velocity gain is most transient in JavaScript/TypeScript and the quality effect strongest in Go, but the authors say this heterogeneity "should not be attributed to the programming languages themselves in our setting" [V], and suspect selection bias (Appendix C, p. 16) [AR]. Rust results are dropped for insufficient observations (Table 7, p. 17) [AE]. Splitting cohorts into Before Agent Release (before November 2024), After Agent Release (after November 2024) and Agent Made Default (after February 2025) shows no qualitative difference in the main findings, except slightly weaker estimated effects on warnings and complexity; the authors say this could reflect model capability gains, selection bias, or most repositories eventually switching to agents (Appendix C, p. 17) [AR]. Footnote 1 reports the same: limiting analyses to these cohorts does not change the main results (§1, fn. 1, p. 2) [AE].

### Alternative estimators (Appendix B, pp. 14–16)

The authors explain that TWFE estimates equal a variance-weighted average of all two-group, two-period DiD estimates only under both the parallel trend and the effect-homogeneity assumptions, and that effect homogeneity is likely violated under staggered adoption (later cohorts may see stronger effects as tools advance), producing "forbidden comparisons" and negative weighting [BT] (Appendix B.1, p. 15). Callaway and Sant'Anna estimate effects within each cohort before aggregating, which avoids cross-cohort contamination but loses power when cohorts are small; many cohorts here have fewer than 100 repositories (Appendix B.2, p. 15) [BT].

For velocity, the three estimators agree qualitatively on the horizon estimates; lines added rise under all three (+28.58% Borusyak, +82.74% TWFE, +53.60% Callaway and Sant'Anna), while commits show small, non-significant effects under Borusyak (+2.63%) and Callaway and Sant'Anna (−0.73%) and a significant +17.83% under TWFE, which the authors say likely reflects forbidden-comparison bias (Appendix B.3, p. 15) [AE]. For quality, Borusyak and TWFE both find significant rises in warnings (+30.26%, +18.48%) and complexity (+41.64%, +26.04%), while Callaway and Sant'Anna gives negative, non-significant estimates (−10.49%, −3.80%); no estimator finds a statistically significant effect on duplicate line density (Appendix B.3, pp. 15–16) [AE]. TWFE shows marginally significant pre-trends for complexity; the other two do not (Appendix B.3, p. 15) [AE].

The authors offer two possible sources of the divergence: small cohorts combined with noisy quality metrics, and Callaway and Sant'Anna conditioning only on pre-treatment covariates while the other two adjust for time-varying ones, adding that there is no clear consensus on when time-varying covariates help or hurt (Appendix B.3, p. 16) [AR]. They report Borusyak in the main paper because it avoids TWFE's biases while pooling untreated observations, passes pre-trend tests on all outcomes, and shows sustained temporal patterns supporting the causal reading (Appendix B.3, p. 16) [AR].

### What the new warnings are (Appendix D, pp. 18–19)

From a convenience sample of 195,010 warnings across 933 SonarQube rules, the first author worked iteratively with Claude Opus 4.5 to build a 20-category taxonomy (Table 9), then estimated new warnings per repository per month before and after adoption, using only months where data were still available as of January 2026 (Appendix D, p. 18) [AE]. Sixteen of 20 categories rose and four fell (Appendix D, p. 18) [AE]. The largest rises were Naming Conventions (+21.32), Code Hygiene (+16.15, leftover artefacts such as commented-out code, TODOs and unused variables), Code Complexity (+15.34) and Code Style (+14.76), with domain-specific rises in Data Science (+11.29), React (+9.52), Type Safety (+8.43) and CSS (+5.68) (Appendix D, Tables 8–9, pp. 18–19) [AE]. The authors say these may come from LLMs trained on low-quality code or from "developers heavily vibe-coding and not rigorously reviewing AI-generated code" [V], with future research needed on the causes (Appendix D, p. 18) [AR].

Logic Errors (+2.09) and Security (+1.98), which the authors call actual bugs both detectable and potentially dangerous, also rose modestly; API Usage (−4.35), Concurrency (−1.95), Resource Management (−0.40) and HTML Structure (−0.26) fell, which they suggest may indicate models trained on recent code proposing more modern APIs and handling some asynchronous patterns better (Appendix D, p. 18) [AR]. Their overall reading is that most new warnings are style and maintainability issues, with non-negligible rises in bad-practice and critical-bug categories, and that "high-velocity AI-powered development generally introduces, rather than resolves, code quality issues" [V] (Appendix D, p. 18) [AR].

## Part V: The authors' interpretation and implications

### Why the velocity gain fades (§5.1.1, p. 10)

The finding that project-level gains concentrate in the first one or two months contrasts with task-level improvements in controlled experiments (§5.1.1, p. 10) [AR]. One reason the authors give is the velocity-quality dynamic visible only longitudinally: higher velocity may grow the codebase and accumulate technical debt, which then slows future velocity (§5.1.1, p. 10) [AR]. They cite prior literature [28, 38] for the negative effect of technical debt on velocity [BT] and report supporting evidence from their own panel GMM models (§5.1.1, p. 10; Table 3, p. 8) [AE]. But "this mechanism alone likely does not fully explain why the development velocity gain vanishes after two months" [V], since full cancellation would need a ∼3x rise in complexity or ∼5x in warnings, "which is unlikely" [V] (§5.1.1, p. 10) [AR].

Their other explanation, which they call highly plausible, is an *excitement-frustration-abandonment cycle*: early on, developers may experience novelty effects and use AI where it excels (e.g. rapid prototyping); then, meeting cases where AI is still limited (debugging intricate logic, understanding existing codebases, handling edge cases), frustration may accumulate, and together with "the cognitive overhead of verifying and debugging AI-generated suggestions" [V] could lead to reduced use or abandonment (§5.1.1, p. 10) [AR]. They say this aligns with emerging qualitative research on developer challenges with AI-assisted coding and with anecdotal evidence from Cursor users [BT] (§5.1.1, p. 10).

### Technical debt and complexity (§5.1.2, p. 10)

The authors present the velocity-quality relationship as one that "challenges simplistic narratives about AI coding degrading code quality" [V] (§5.1.2, p. 10) [AR]. Although warnings rise, much of that effect follows the path of higher velocity to a larger codebase to more technical debt (Table 3); in their words, "LLM agent assistants amplify existing velocity-quality dynamics by enabling faster code production" [V], and may not introduce more quality issues than non-adopting projects moving at the same velocity (§5.1.2, p. 10) [AR]. This proportional relationship implies "that quality assurance needs to scale with AI-era velocity" [V]; citing a Pluralistic post, they add that AI does not change the fact "that all code is a liability and the asset lies only in the code’s capabilities" [V] (§5.1.2, p. 10) [BT].

Complexity is treated as a distinct dimension. That it rises even after accounting for velocity "gives strong evidence that code generated with Cursor in our study sample is inherently more complex than human-written code" [V], creating a "complexity debt" [V] in projects that use AI heavily, which may amplify frustration and maintenance costs when the AI later fails on more complex codebases, possibly another mechanism behind the transient velocity gain (§5.1.2, p. 10) [AR]. Duplicate line density shows no significant change in the whole sample, though heavy adopters may show modest rises (Figure 4); more research is needed (§5.1.2, p. 10) [AR].

### Open-source context (§5.1.3, pp. 10–11)

"Our findings should be interpreted within the specific context of open-source software development" [V], which the authors say differs from enterprise settings in four ways: voluntary participation with low switching costs, which makes abandonment easy; distributed collaboration, potentially reducing systematic code review that might catch AI-introduced defects; intrinsic motivation and learning goals, where experimenting has value beyond productivity; and resource constraints limiting testing and quality assurance (§5.1.3, p. 10) [AR]. These likely amplify the excitement-frustration-abandonment cycle while potentially dampening the quality feedback loop (§5.1.3, pp. 10–11) [AR]. In enterprises, the authors suggest that mandates, sunk training costs and managerial oversight might sustain AI tool use despite user frustration, potentially leading to distinct temporal patterns (§5.1.3, p. 11) [AR]; they cite Kumar et al. [73] as indicating such distinct temporal patterns (§5.1.3, p. 11) [BT]. They also suggest that mandatory code review, automated testing, dedicated QA teams and dedicated maintenance agents might prevent proportional debt accumulation (§5.1.3, p. 11) [AR]. Whether the patterns generalize to enterprises is left to future research (§5.1.3, p. 11) [AR].

### Practical implications (§5.2, p. 11)

*Process.* "To overcome the technical debt accumulation ratchet" [V], projects using agent assistants should adapt their process to scale quality assurance with AI-era velocity; the authors suggest refactoring sprints triggered by code quality metrics, test coverage requirements that scale with lines added, and prompt engineering such as engineered Cursor rules to enforce quality standards (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. "Without such adaptations, the initial productivity surge may accelerate the project toward an unmaintainable end state." [V] (§5.2, p. 11).

*Tools.* The LLM agents of the study period "are generation-first, leaving quality maintenance as an afterthought" [V] (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. Future assistants should suggest tests alongside code, flag unnecessary complexity in real time and recommend refactoring when quality degrades, becoming "pair programmers" for quality as well as velocity; more provocatively, tools might self-throttle, reducing suggestion volume or aggressiveness when project complexity or debt exceeds healthy thresholds, forcing developers to consolidate before generating more (§5.2, p. 11) [AR].

*Complexity.* The authors call the complexity increase a "comprehension tax" [V] that persists regardless of functional correctness, suggesting LLMs may generate "structurally valid but semantically opaque code" [V], perhaps because training objectives favour passing tests over non-functional requirements such as readability [BT] (§5.2, p. 11). Unless workflows allow fully automated development without human code review, readability stays important; addressing it needs technical work (readability-aware fine-tuning, post-hoc simplification) and research into why LLMs over-complicate (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. Until then, teams "should treat AI-generated code as requiring extra scrutiny during review" [V], checking whether simpler implementations exist (§5.2, p. 11) [AR].

### Conclusion (§6, p. 11)

The authors describe the study as the first large-scale empirical investigation of how LLM agent assistants affect real-world software projects, and its results as suggesting "a self-reinforcing cycle where initial productivity surges give way to maintenance burdens" [V] (§6, p. 11) [AR]. They give three reasons the picture may be less bleak: it is a snapshot of technology from mid-2024 to mid-2025, when capabilities and practices were improving fast and future tools might address the quality concerns; their quality metrics may not fully capture code quality in AI-driven development; and the open-source context may amplify abandonment and quality concerns relative to enterprises with mandatory, dedicated QA (§6, p. 11) [AR]. Realizing the promise of AI-assisted development, they close, needs a holistic understanding of how AI reshapes trade-offs between velocity, quality and long-term sustainability (§6, p. 11) [AR].

### The theory diagram (Figure 1, p. 1)

Figure 1 sets out the authors' theory: "Solid lines indicate causal relationships supported by our analysis; dashed lines indicate partial evidence; and dotted lines indicate inconclusive evidence." [V] (Figure 1, p. 1). Read from the render: the LLM agent assistant raises development velocity (solid, +), static analysis warnings (dashed, +) and code complexity (solid, +), with a dotted "?" to duplicate line density; these three sit in a dotted box labelled "Technical Debt / Quality Measures", and warnings and complexity each lower development velocity (solid, −) (Figure 1, p. 1) [AE].

## Connections the author makes in the text

- Becker et al. [27], controlled experiments with early-2025 AI tools including Cursor: cited as showing no speed-up for experienced open-source developers and over-optimism; used to frame the gap between tool generations [BT] (§1, p. 2; §2, p. 3).
- Watanabe et al. [110], 567 Claude Code pull requests: cited as an important step whose focus on acceptance rates leaves project-level effects open [BT] (§1, p. 2).
- Earlier Copilot productivity studies, among them Peng et al. [94], Song et al. [102], Cui et al. [40], Pandey et al. [91], Yeverechyahu et al. [111] and Daniotti et al. [43]: cited neutrally for the prior range of productivity estimates; Yeverechyahu et al. named as the closest prior causal study [BT] (§2, p. 3).
- Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess [29]: the imputation estimator the main analysis uses [BT] (§3.3.3, p. 6).
- Callaway and Sant'Anna [31] and two-way fixed effects: alternative estimators reported in Appendix B; TWFE criticized, via Goodman-Bacon [54], De Chaisemartin and d'Haultfoeuille [44] and Athey and Imbens [23], for bias under staggered adoption [BT] (§3.3.3, p. 6; Appendix B, pp. 14–16).
- Arellano and Bond [22]: the dynamic panel GMM method and its validity tests [BT] (§3.4, p. 6; §4.2, p. 8).
- Austin [24, 25, 26], Caliendo and Kopeinig [30], Stuart et al. [106]: propensity score matching and balance conventions [BT] (§3.1.3, pp. 4–5; Appendix A, p. 14).
- Campbell [32] and SonarQube: cognitive complexity as the complexity metric, preferred to McCabe's cyclomatic complexity [82] [BT] (§3.2.1, p. 5).
- Munaiah et al. [84]: the 10-star threshold's 97% precision for engineered projects [BT] (§3.1.2, p. 4).
- Besker et al. [28] and Cheng et al. [38]: cited in support of technical debt reducing productivity and velocity-quality interaction [BT] (§3.4, p. 6; §5.1.1, p. 10).
- Kumar et al. [73]: an enterprise study indicating different temporal patterns of AI tool use [BT] (§5.1.3, p. 11).
- GitClear's "Coding on Copilot" data [6]: cited as an example of the simplistic narrative the authors' findings challenge [BT] (§5.1.2, p. 10).
- Pluralistic, "Code is a liability (not an asset)" [13]: cited for the point that all code is a liability [BT] (§5.1.2, p. 10).
- Gureja et al. [57] and Zheng et al. [112]: cited for training objectives favouring passing tests over non-functional requirements [BT] (§5.2, p. 11).
- Chen et al. [37], Liang et al. [76] and Becker et al. [27]; dev.to and Arsturn posts [9, 11]: qualitative research and anecdote cited as aligning with the abandonment explanation [BT] (§5.1.1, p. 10).
- Reddit r/cursor survey [15] and a blog post on 10x productivity [10]: cited as self-reported multifold claims [BT] (§1, p. 1; §2, p. 3).
- Martin, *Clean Code* [80]: cited for the technical-debt perspective on quality [BT] (§3.2.1, p. 5).
- 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey [2]: 76% using or planning to use LLM tools [BT] (§2, p. 2).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Unbridled optimism about AI-assisted coding.* The authors say empirical evidence is lacking around self-reported multifold productivity claims and describe gray-literature estimates as orders of magnitude larger than any empirical estimate for prior tools (Abstract, p. 1; §2, p. 3); they present their evidence as challenging "unbridled optimism" (§6, p. 11).
- *Carrying findings on completion and chat tools over to agentic assistants.* The architectural difference has implications that cannot be extrapolated from prior studies (§1, p. 1).
- *Simplistic narratives about AI coding degrading code quality.* Much of the warning increase follows velocity and codebase growth; the authors present their evidence as challenging "categorical pessimism" too (§5.1.2, p. 10; §6, p. 11).
- *Two-way fixed effects for staggered adoption.* May produce biased estimates when effects vary over time, which is why the main analysis uses the Borusyak estimator (§3.3.3, p. 6; Appendix B.1, p. 15).
- *Generation-first tool design.* Agents that leave quality maintenance as an afterthought; the authors call for tools explicitly designed to support quality assurance alongside generation (§5.2, p. 11).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

**Conversion.** The original is the 19-page arXiv PDF (v3, created 2026-01-27 by arXiv GenPDF; sha256 9ad060acc8f3321e883fcf63928bfeac4a58be3ea4dce7986d6f59464c334da9), fetched 2026-10-11 from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.04427v3. The tape `sources/converted/he-cursor-velocity-complexity-2025.md` (3,052 lines, 17,912 words) is `pdftotext` (poppler 26.08.0) default reading-order output, run one page at a time with a `{page-N}` marker before each page. Post-conversion check: 19 markers, folios 1–19 present, Table 9's last row present at the end, no truncation marker; about 940 words a page.

**Page anchors.** `{page-N}` markers at tape lines 1, 122, 227, 333, 644, 756, 889, 1006, 1215, 1440, 1543, 1643, 1801, 1956, 2173, 2317, 2501, 2744 and 2892 for pp. 1–19.

**Reading order and tables.** The two-column layout interleaves in places (on p. 2 the research question comes after text that follows it on the page; §3.1.2 and §3.1.3 alternate on p. 4; §5.1.1 and §5.1.2 alternate on p. 10). Quotations here are taken only from contiguous runs. Tables 1–8 are extracted column by column, so values were read against `pdftotext -layout` output. The default-mode text corrupts the significance annotations: Table 2 attaches three stars to all five coefficient estimates; Table 3 attaches three stars to coefficients, standard errors and diagnostic entries, Num. Obs. included; and Table 6 attaches three stars to all Borusyak and TWFE coefficients and two stars to all Callaway and Sant'Anna coefficients. Significance levels recorded here come from the renders of pp. 7, 8 and 16 (Table 2: commits and duplicate density unstarred, lines added one star, warnings and complexity three; Table 3: both lines-added → quality main effects and Cursor → warnings unstarred, Cursor → complexity two stars, the remaining coefficient estimates three; Table 6: Borusyak stars match Table 2, TWFE duplicate density unstarred and its other coefficients three stars, Callaway and Sant'Anna lines added two stars and its other coefficients unstarred). Figure 2–7 values are not recorded beyond what the text states. Words broken at line ends lost their hyphen in the tape (e.g. "selfthrottling", "excitement-frustrationabandonment", "nonadopting"); those terms are paraphrased here, not quoted.

**Values that differ across passages, as printed.** The average code complexity increase is 41% (§1), +41.64% (Table 2) and 41.6% (§4.1.2), but "25.1%, Table 2" in §5.1.2 and "The 25% increase in code complexity we observe (Table 3)" in §5.2; this reference uses the Table 2 value. The treatment sample is 806 repositories (§3.1.2) and the matched controls 1,380 (§1), while Table 7's "Original" setting lists 801 treatment and 1,172 control repositories. Appendix A cites "balance checks (Figure 5)" for the content of Table 5; Appendix B.1 points to "Section 3.1.3" for the ATT definitions given in §3.3.2; Table 5's caption says Table 1 reflects metrics "at the time of data analysis", while Table 1's caption says "data collection (April 2025)".

**Spellings kept as printed.** Not quoted here: "execeptions" (p. 3), "covarates" (p. 4), "remainig" (p. 6), "distangle" (p. 8), "Follwing" (p. 14), "manitudes" (p. 15), "Feburary" and "pprogramminglanguage" (p. 17), "Orginal" in figure legends (pp. 9, 17).

**Provenance stated in the paper.** Funding: National Science Foundation awards 2206859, 2317168 and 2120323 and Graduate Research Fellowship DGE214073; research awards from Google and the Digital Infrastructure Fund; Google Cloud research credits for BigQuery analysis (p. 11). The Appendix D taxonomy was generated by the first author working iteratively with Claude Opus 4.5 (p. 18).

**Licence and scope.** CC BY 4.0 per the first-page notice; scope `open`. Short `[V]` quotations here are checked against the tape.

**What this reference does not carry.** Nothing from the cited works beyond how the authors cite them; no Figure 2–7 values beyond those the text states; no claims about the authors beyond their affiliations and the funding they list.
